episodes.213156: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
episodes.213238: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
episodes.213539: The afternoon of June 24th, scattered strong to severe storms developed in southern Wisconsin and Illinois. A few of these storms become supercell thunderstorms, with isolated reports of damaging winds in northwest Illinois.
episodes.213606: A weak low-pressure center over northwest North Dakota progressed southeast into Minnesota on June 23rd. Increased moisture advection ahead of a surface cold front would aid in the development of thunderstorms across the southern half of Minnesota by late morning. Mixed layer instability combined with sufficient wind shear did manage to support a few cells to produce large hail. Hail stones mainly ranged between quarter to golf ball size. The largest hailstone measured was 2.5 inches 6 miles NNW of Cosmos (Meeker County). Farther to the southeast in Rice County, a brief funnel cloud developed between Faribault and Kenyon but was never reported as reaching the ground.
episodes.213692: Thunderstorms developed over central and southern Wyoming and became severe late in the afternoon through the late evening hours of June 24th. Large hail and strong gusty winds were reported.
episodes.213989: Thunderstorms moved east and southeast into eastern Oklahoma during the morning and early afternoon of the 24th. Locally heavy rainfall occurred in some places, which resulted in isolated flash flooding.
episodes.214019: A cold frontal boundary progressed across the southeastern states on the 23rd of June before slowing progress and nearly stalling over the northeast FL/southeast GA region. Plenty of summer moisture and instability in the vicinity of the boundary resulted in numerous to widespread showers and thunderstorms for several days in a row.
episodes.214355: Scattered heavy thunderstorms developed across north-central Oklahoma during the early to mid-morning hours of the 24th. Provided slow movement and heavy rainfall rates, scattered flooding occurred, especially across far eastern Payne County, Oklahoma.
episodes.214470: Clusters of strong thunderstorms along the coast produced a few measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.214483: Scattered thunderstorms developed and tracked east across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail was the main storm threat with three inch diameter hail being reported near Wiggins.

episodes.214529: Thunderstorms developed across the Northland during the midday and early afternoon hours of the 24th as an area of low pressure moved through the region. Most of the storms remained below severe limits, but one storm did produce quarter-sized hail in central Douglas County.
episodes.214608: A stationary front was stalled over the coastal Mississippi.  At the same time, a weak upper level trough was moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley.  Both of these features tapped into a warm and unstable airmass to produce thunderstorm activity in coastal Mississippi.  These thunderstorms produced some severe wind gusts.
episodes.214609: A stationary front was stalled just onshore. At the same time, a weak upper level trough was moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley. Both of these features tapped into a warm and unstable airmass to produce thunderstorm activity in the coastal waters. These thunderstorms produced a waterspout and a marine thunderstorm wind event.
episodes.214661: A typical summertime pattern produced scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms with occasional severe weather reported.

episodes.215305: Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-6+ inches fell over Southern McCurtain County Oklahoma from the morning through the evening, contributing to areas of flash flooding. An isolated severe thunderstorm also developed over this area during the evening hours on the 23rd before diminishing. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across McCurtain County Oklahoma along with an isolated damaging wind report.
episodes.215307: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and early evening on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, extending along the Middle Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across the area, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, extending well into the afternoon and early evening. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. As a result, several damaging wind reports were recorded across parts of Southwest Arkansas.
episodes.215308: Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6+ inches fell over portions of Northeast Texas during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the afternoon, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across Northeast Texas along with a few damaging wind reports.
episodes.215361: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley of Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and into extreme Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning hours of June 23rd, which focused areas of repeated showers and thunderstorms as an upper level disturbance shifted east-southeast atop the front. A very warm and moist air mass resided near and south of the front, which contributed to increased storm intensity and rain rates with areas of heavy rainfall falling over extreme Northeast Texas and North Louisiana during the morning. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-10+ inches fell over portions of North Louisiana during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the evening through the morning hours on the 24th, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-4+ inches falling. These storms also spawned an isolated tornado near Plain Dealing during the evening of the 23rd.
episodes.215506: A weakening mesoscale convective system (MCS) advanced east southeast into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours on June 24th, just north of an outflow reinforced frontal boundary which extended from Northeast Texas into North Central Louisiana and eastward into Mississippi. Behind the MCS, showers and thunderstorms increased in coverage from North Louisiana into Southwest Arkansas. Wind profiles in the 925-850 millibar layer showed some modest strengthening into the 25-30 knot range from the south southwest, helping to remove lingering lower level convective inhibition centered near 850 mb. Low level flow overrunning the surface boundary set up a convergence axis in the 925-850 millibar layer, aligned from Southeast Oklahoma into Northwest Louisiana. This zone of convergence focused increasing coverage of elevated thunderstorms throughout the morning, beneath increasingly diffluent flow aloft in the 300-400 millibar layer. The convergence axis was aligned with a gradient in MLCAPE of 500 to 1500 J/kg noted to the southwest of the axis. Precipitable water (PWAT) values ranged from 1.7 to near 2 inches across the region. As a result, hourly rainfall rates of 1 to 2+ inches occurred within areas of training storms with localized rainfall totals of 2 to 6+ inches common across Southwest Arkansas. Thus, numerous reports of flash flooding were recorded throughout the morning into the mid-afternoon.
episodes.215536: Several supercell thunderstorms developed within the warm sector of a broad surface low over central Wisconsin. The clusters of storms tracked southeastward through south central Wisconsin during the afternoon and early evening. Sporadic wind damage to trees and power lines occurred including hail around one inch in diameter.

A weak EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 88 mph was spawned during the evening hours of June 23, 2026, from a quasi-linear convective line segment passing through and near the community of Plain Dealing. A vast majority of the damage was to trees with many hardwood and softwood trees being uprooted along the path. Sporadic softwood tree snaps throughout the assessed path of nearly 5 miles long garnered the peak wind speed of 88 mph for the tornado. Many power lines were downed in the path of the tornado, but the survey team determined that most of this occurrence was due to trees and tree limbs falling on the lines. It is also important to note that there were other sporadic instances of tree damage throughout northern Bossier Parish was due to the severe line of thunderstorms moving through during the evening, but the assessed tornado damage featured much more concentrated damage along a path.
